source.title: DB-KSVD: Scalable Alternating Optimization for Disentangling High-Dimensional Embedding Spaces
source.authors: Romeo Valentin; Sydney M. Katz; Vincent Vanhoucke; M. Kochenderfer

record.file_problem: None noted; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study evaluates dictionary learning on embeddings from language models, an LLM setting, and also vision models. Its results bear indirectly on whether learned dictionaries recover useful sparse features in real-model embeddings, rather than reproducing the original toy-model experiments.
record.gate_note: The paper reports benchmark outcomes, dictionary coherence measurements, and vision-model evaluation results. Theorems and background claims about sparsity, identifiability, and superposition are not experimental results. The figures provide many values only graphically; the text gives aggregate comparisons for the Gemma SAEBench results. The study does not directly test feature ground-truth recovery or whether features are distributed across neurons.
record.test_reason: A methods paper. Superposition is the premise for dictionary learning, and the results benchmark the authors' DB-KSVD against SAE variants on SAEBench and DINOv2 metrics. There is no ground-truth feature recovery and no non-dictionary control (neuron basis, random dictionary). So the rows measure relative method performance, not whether models contain recoverable sparse features (V4) or whether dictionary features are canonical (V5).
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that KSVD-style alternating optimization scales to interpretability-sized problems and matches SAEs across models and modalities. They suggest both methods may be near theoretical limits on these metrics, and that coherence explains the autointerpretability and absorption trends. Their stated caveat is narrower than the record's: it is unclear whether scaling to millions of samples is enough to solve disentanglement.
record.recipe_differences: The study learns sparse dictionaries from pretrained model embeddings using Matching Pursuit and alternating KSVD updates; it does not train the original toy networks or reproduce their feature-generation setup.
record.method_sensitivity: Reported outcomes vary with metric and method: Matryoshka structuring reduces dictionary coherence and improves autointerpretability and absorption while slightly degrading loss recovered and SCR. In vision, DB-KSVD is stronger on variance explained and autointerpretability, while SAE is stronger on sparse probing.

fits_no_version.finding: On Gemma-2-2B layer 12 (m=4096 and 16384) and Pythia-160M, DB-KSVD beats the Standard ReLU SAE on most SAEBench metrics and is competitive with other SAE variants. The exception is autointerpretability, where it falls short.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Alternating-optimization dictionary learning (KSVD) reaches SAE-level SAEBench performance on LLM embeddings.

fits_no_version.finding: On DINOv2-S/B, DB-KSVD scores higher than a TopK SAE on variance explained and autointerpretability. The SAE scores higher on sparse probing.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Relative quality of sparse dictionaries on vision embeddings depends on the evaluation metric.

fits_no_version.finding: DB-KSVD dictionaries are highly coherent at small k, with a spike of near-identical atoms. Matryoshka structuring reduces coherence, and m=16384 dictionaries are less coherent.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The coherence of learned LLM dictionaries varies with sparsity, dictionary size and structuring.

record.problems: The LLM feature-quality evidence is indirect: there is no ground-truth feature set or direct measure of recovery of the model's actual features. Many plotted comparisons are not numerically stated in the text, and the text does not identify the sparse-probing instance where DB-KSVD fails to outperform Standard ReLU SAE. No uncertainty estimates are stated for the reported benchmark values.
record.rows_left_out: No reported result rows omitted. The DINOv2 Table 5 extended sparse-probing results are omitted because they repeat the sparse-probing metric at additional ksp settings and are outside the LLM-specific claim version; the principal DINOv2 Table 4 results are retained.

untested.parts: No toy networks, sparsity phase transition or toy geometry.
No neuron polysemanticity or importance-vs-capacity measurement.
No ground-truth recovery, no neuron-basis or random-dictionary control, and no measure of feature spread across neurons. The benchmarks only rank dictionary methods against each other.
Two methods reach similar benchmark scores, but the dictionaries are not compared atom-by-atom. No stability, completeness or canonicality test.
Atoms are assumed to be 1-D. No test against multi-dimensional features.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's 'tests/T3' and V4 labels are withdrawn. All rows compare the authors' method with other dictionary methods, which the rules treat as the study's own method's performance. The superposition hypothesis is assumed as motivation, not tested. The m=16384 SAEBench results (Fig 5/6) and Table 5 are not rowed, but they are also method comparisons only.

versions.untested_parts: No small toy networks, sparsity-dependent transition, or regular toy-model feature geometry are tested.
The study does not measure neuron polysemanticity or test whether feature importance determines dedicated versus shared capacity.
The study does not investigate alternative causes of polysemantic neurons.

Tests dictionary quality on language-model embeddings indirectly through benchmark metrics, not ground-truth feature recovery or feature distribution across neurons. The vision-model results are recorded separately because this version specifies LLMs.
No completeness, stability, or canonicality test of SAE or dictionary features.
Dictionary atoms are represented as directions, but the study does not compare one-dimensional features with multidimensional features or test whether actual model features are one-dimensional.

rows.subject: Gemma-2-2B
rows.operation_detail: Evaluated DB-KSVD dictionaries against SAE methods on SAEBench loss recovered.
rows.baseline: Standard ReLU SAE and other SAE variants
rows.value: Figure only; text says DB-KSVD outperforms Standard ReLU SAE and is generally competitive with the other SAE variants.
rows.note: The text gives aggregate comparisons, not exact metric values for each sparsity.
rows.check: Compares the study's own method (DB-KSVD) with SAE baselines on loss recovered. It does not measure whether the LLM has sparse features. Values are figure-only.

rows.subject: Gemma-2-2B
rows.operation_detail: Evaluated DB-KSVD dictionaries against SAE methods on SAEBench autointerpretability.
rows.value: Figure only; text says DB-KSVD does not match the other SAE variants on autointerpretability.
rows.note: The Matryoshka DB-KSVD adaptation improves this metric, but the text does not give exact values.
rows.check: Own-method vs SAE comparison on autointerpretability. 'Partial' describes DB-KSVD trailing the SAEs, not any version's effect.

rows.subject: Gemma-2-2B
rows.operation_detail: Evaluated DB-KSVD dictionaries against SAE methods on SAEBench absorption.
rows.baseline: Standard ReLU SAE and other SAE variants
rows.value: Figure only; text says DB-KSVD outperforms Standard ReLU SAE and is generally competitive with the other SAE variants.
rows.note: Matryoshka structuring improves absorption but slightly degrades some other reported metrics.
rows.check: Own-method vs SAE comparison on absorption. This is not a test of V4.

rows.subject: Gemma-2-2B
rows.operation_detail: Evaluated DB-KSVD dictionaries against SAE methods on SAEBench sparse probing.
rows.baseline: Standard ReLU SAE and other SAE variants
rows.value: Figure only; text says DB-KSVD outperforms Standard ReLU SAE except in one instance and is generally competitive with other SAE variants.
rows.note: The text does not identify which instance is the exception.
rows.check: Own-method vs SAE comparison on sparse probing. The one exception relates to the Standard ReLU SAE only.

rows.subject: Pythia-160M
rows.operation_detail: Compared DB-KSVD dictionaries with SAE baselines on available SAEBench metrics.
rows.measure: Overall comparison on available SAEBench metrics
rows.value: Figure only; text says the results show trends similar to those for Gemma-2-2B.
rows.note: The text does not specify the outcome metric by metric. RAVEL comparisons are not shown because the authors were unable to find baseline data files.
rows.check: Own-method vs SAE comparison on Pythia-160M. The text says only 'similar trends'.

rows.subject: Gemma-2-2B
rows.operation_detail: Measured element-wise dictionary coherence across sparsity settings.
rows.measure: Maximum absolute inner product of each dictionary element with other elements
rows.baseline: SAE dictionaries constructed for the same problem
rows.value: Figure only; text says DB-KSVD dictionaries are relatively coherent, especially at smaller k, and include a notable spike of almost perfectly aligned elements.
rows.note: This is a geometry result on learned language-model dictionaries, not a test of the toy-model geometry or the dimensionality of underlying features.

rows.subject: Gemma-2-2B
rows.operation_detail: Applied Matryoshka structuring to DB-KSVD dictionary learning and measured the resulting coherence.
rows.value: Figure only; text says Matryoshka structuring significantly decreases coherence.
rows.note: The paper also reports a similar decrease when Matryoshka structuring is applied to SAE dictionaries.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Gemma-2-2B embeddings, dictionary size m = 4096; reported SAEBench metrics other than autointerpretability and the one sparse-probing instance
reader_labels.reason: DB-KSVD performs competitively with SAE approaches on several feature-quality metrics, supporting dictionary-based recovery as indirect evidence; see r1, r3, r5, and r6.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Gemma-2-2B embeddings, dictionary size m = 4096; autointerpretability and sparse probing
reader_labels.reason: DB-KSVD falls short of the other SAE variants on autointerpretability, and the text reports one sparse-probing exception to its advantage over Standard ReLU SAE; see r2 and r4.
